about: The scripted AI lesson for p5-fluid-pressure (2026-11-28, Phase C, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-27-phase-c-physics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p5-moments and p3-density.

keyPoints.heading: Pressure in a fluid: p = F/A

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about how liquids and gases push on things: why your ears hurt at the bottom of a pool, and why a ship floats.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from earlier lessons. A 40 N force acts 0.5 m from a pivot. What is its moment?

wrong.divide: Not quite: multiply the force by the distance: 40 × 0.5 = 20 Nm.
wrong.add: Not quite: multiply, do not add: 40 × 0.5 = 20 Nm.

idk.hint: Moment = force × distance from the pivot: 40 × 0.5.

steps.question: Second: a block has a mass of 2 kg and a volume of 0.001 m³. What is its density?

wrong.times: Not quite: divide the mass by the volume: 2 ÷ 0.001 = 2000 kg/m³.
wrong.flip: Not quite: divide the mass by the volume, not the other way round: 2 ÷ 0.001 = 2000 kg/m³.

steps.text: Now this lesson. A liquid or a gas is called a fluid, because it can flow.
A fluid is made of tiny particles that move about and hit every surface they touch, from every side: up, down and sideways.
The particles' hits push on each surface at right angles to it. At right angles to a surface is called normal to it.
The force on each square metre of a surface is called the pressure. The equation is p = F ÷ A: pressure = force normal to a surface ÷ area of that surface.
F is the force in newtons (N) and A is the area in square metres (m²). Pressure p is measured in a unit called the pascal (Pa): 1 Pa is 1 N/m².
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: A box pushes on the floor with a force of 600 N. The face it rests on is 0.2 m by 0.1 m. What is the pressure?
steps: Write the equation: p = F ÷ A.

steps.question: Your turn. A box weighs 500 N, so it pushes on the floor with 500 N. The face it rests on is 0.5 m long and 0.4 m wide. What pressure does it put on the floor, in Pa?
steps.right: Yes: the area is 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2 m², and 500 ÷ 0.2 = 2500 Pa.

wrong.other: Not quite: 2500 Pa. Area = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2 m², and p = 500 ÷ 0.2 = 2500 Pa.
wrong.times: Not quite: 2500 Pa. Divide the force by the area: 500 ÷ 0.2 = 2500 Pa.
wrong.length: Not quite: 2500 Pa. Use the area of the face, 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2 m², not one length. Then 500 ÷ 0.2 = 2500 Pa.

idk.hint: First find the area of the face: length × width. Then p = F ÷ A.

steps.question: The same person stands in flat trainers, then in narrow high heels. When is the pressure on the floor bigger?
steps.right: Yes: the same force on a smaller area gives a bigger pressure.

wrong.other: Not quite: in the high heels.
wrong.trainers: Not quite: trainers spread the force over a bigger area, so the pressure is smaller. Heels give the bigger pressure.
wrong.same: Not quite: the force is the same, but the heels have a smaller area, so the pressure is bigger.

idk.hint: The weight is the same both times. Which shoes have the smaller area touching the floor?

steps.answerWhy: The force is the same, but the heels touch a smaller area, so p = F ÷ A is bigger.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is pressure?
points: Pressure is the force on each square metre of a surface: force ÷ area
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: pressure is the force normal to a surface divided by the area of that surface.

keyPoints.heading: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth

steps.text: Dive to the bottom of a pool and your ears feel the pressure. The deeper you go, the taller the column of water above you, the water stacked straight above you. So more weight of water pushes down.
Density is how much mass is packed into each cubic metre. A denser liquid has more mass in each column, so more weight above the same point: more pressure.
The equation is p = h ρ g: pressure = height of the column × density of the liquid × gravitational field strength (gravity's pull on each kilogram).
p is in pascals and h, the height, in metres (m). ρ, the Greek letter rho, is the density in kg/m³, and g is in N/kg.
You are given this equation in the exam.
Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: In a pool, water has a density of 1000 kg/m³, and g = 9.8 N/kg. What is the pressure due to the water 2 m below the surface?
steps: Write the equation: p = h ρ g.

steps.question: Your turn. What is the pressure due to the water 5 m below the surface in the same pool, in Pa?

wrong.nog: Not quite: 49 000 Pa. Remember to multiply by g as well: 5 × 1000 × 9.8 = 49 000 Pa.
wrong.two: Not quite: 19 600 Pa is the pressure at 2 m. At 5 m: 5 × 1000 × 9.8 = 49 000 Pa.

idk.hint: Use p = h ρ g with h = 5.

steps.question: What is the difference in pressure between 2 m and 5 m below the surface, in Pa?

wrong.deep: Not quite: 49 000 Pa is the pressure at 5 m. Take away the pressure at 2 m: 49 000 − 19 600 = 29 400 Pa.
wrong.add: Not quite: a difference means subtract: 49 000 − 19 600 = 29 400 Pa.

idk.hint: Take the pressure at 2 m away from the pressure at 5 m.

steps.question: Three containers, one wide, one narrow and one that widens at the top, are filled with water to the same depth. Where is the pressure at the bottom biggest?

options.text: It is the same in all three

steps.right: Yes: the pressure depends on the depth and the density, not the shape.

wrong.other: Not quite: it is the same in all three.
wrong.wide: Not quite: the pressure at a point depends only on the depth of water above it and the water's density, not on the container's shape. Same depth, same pressure.
wrong.narrow: Not quite: the pressure at a point depends only on the depth of water above it and the water's density, not on the container's shape. Same depth, same pressure.

idk.hint: Look at p = h ρ g. Is there anything in it about the shape of the container?

steps.answerWhy: Pressure depends only on depth, density and g, so at the same depth of water the pressure is the same in all three.

steps.prompt: In one line: why is the pressure bigger deeper in a liquid?
points: Deeper down there is a taller column of liquid above, so more weight pushes down
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: pressure is bigger deeper in a liquid because there is a taller column of liquid above, so more weight pushes down on each square metre.

steps.question: A brick held under water is pushed upwards by the water. Where do you think that upward push comes from?

options.text: The pressure on its bottom is bigger than on its top
The brick loses weight under water

steps.right: Yes: its bottom is deeper, so the pressure there is bigger, giving an overall force upwards.

wrong.other: Not quite: the pressure on its bottom is bigger than on its top.
wrong.up: Not quite: water pushes on every surface, from every side. The push up on the bottom is bigger than the push down on the top.
wrong.weight: Not quite: the brick's weight does not change. The water pushes up on its bottom harder than down on its top.

idk.hint: The bottom of the brick is deeper than its top, and pressure is bigger deeper down.

steps.answerWhy: The bottom is deeper, so the pressure there is bigger than on the top, which gives an overall force upwards.

steps.text: The upward push comes from depth. An object's bottom surface is deeper than its top surface, so the water pushes up on the bottom harder than it pushes down on the top.
The difference between the two pushes gives an overall force upwards on the object. This upward force from a liquid or a gas is called upthrust.
Push an object further under and its bottom goes deeper, so the upthrust grows, until the object is fully under.
An object floats when the upthrust equals its weight. If its weight is still bigger once it is fully under, it sinks.

steps.question: A large log floats, but a small stone sinks. Why do you think that is?

options.text: The log is less dense than water; the stone is denser
The stone is heavier than the log

steps.right: Yes: floating depends on density, not size.

wrong.other: Not quite: the log is less dense than water, and the stone is denser.
wrong.big: Not quite: big things can sink too, like a large rock. It depends on density: the log is less dense than water.
wrong.heavy: Not quite: the log is heavier than the stone. What matters is density: the log is less dense than water, the stone denser.

idk.hint: Is it about size, or about how much mass is packed into each bit?

steps.answerWhy: Floating depends on density: the log is less dense than water, so it floats, and the stone is denser, so it sinks.

steps.text: Density decides it. An object less dense than the liquid floats; an object denser than the liquid sinks. A steel ship floats because, with the air inside, it is less dense than water overall.

steps.prompt: In one line: when does an object float?
points: An object floats when the upthrust equals its weight
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: an object floats when the upthrust equals its weight, which happens when it is less dense than the liquid.

steps.text: The thin layer of air round the Earth is called the atmosphere. It is very thin compared with the size of the Earth.
Air is made of particles called molecules. They are always hitting every surface, and their hits make a pressure called atmospheric pressure.

steps.question: A climber goes up a high mountain. What do you think the air pressure is like at the top?
steps.right: Yes: it is lower. The next message explains why.

wrong.higher: Not quite: it is lower at the top. The next message explains why.
wrong.same: Not quite: it is lower at the top. The next message explains why.

idk.hint: At the top, is there more or less air above the climber?

steps.answerWhy: At the top of the mountain there is less air above, so less weight of air and a lower pressure.

steps.text: Higher up, there is less air above a surface, so the weight of air above it is smaller. So atmospheric pressure falls as height increases.
The air is also less dense higher up: fewer molecules in each cubic metre, so fewer hits on each surface.

steps.prompt: In one line: why does air pressure fall as you go higher?
points: Higher up there is less air above, so less weight of air pushes down
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: air pressure falls as you go higher because there is less air above, so a smaller weight of air pushes down.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: which unit is pressure measured in?

wrong.newton: Not quite: newtons measure force. Pressure is in pascals.
wrong.nm: Not quite: newton-metres measure moments. Pressure is in pascals.

idk.hint: The unit is named after Blaise Pascal, a French scientist.

steps.answerWhy: Pressure is measured in pascals (Pa): 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: a force of 100 N acts on an area of 0.5 m². What is the pressure?

wrong.times: Not quite: divide the force by the area: 100 ÷ 0.5 = 200 Pa.
wrong.add: Not quite: you added. Divide the force by the area: 100 ÷ 0.5 = 200 Pa.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: water has a density of 1000 kg/m³, and g = 9.8 N/kg. What is the pressure due to the water 3 m down?

wrong.nog: Not quite: multiply by g too: 3 × 1000 × 9.8 = 29 400 Pa.
wrong.noh: Not quite: multiply by the depth too: 3 × 1000 × 9.8 = 29 400 Pa.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 6: which two things make the pressure in a liquid bigger?

options.text: More depth and a denser liquid
A wider container and more depth
Less depth and a denser liquid

steps.right: Yes: p = h ρ g, so more depth or more density means more pressure.

wrong.other: Not quite: more depth and a denser liquid.
wrong.wide: Not quite: the width does not matter. Depth and density do.
wrong.less: Not quite: less depth gives less pressure. More depth and a denser liquid give more.

idk.hint: Look at p = h ρ g.

steps.answerWhy: p = h ρ g, so a greater depth (h) or a denser liquid (ρ) gives a bigger pressure.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: which of these floats in water?

options.text: An object less dense than water

steps.right: Yes: an object less dense than water floats.

wrong.other: Not quite: an object less dense than water.
wrong.large: Not quite: a large rock still sinks. It depends on density: less dense than water floats.
wrong.heavy: Not quite: a heavy log can float. It depends on density: less dense than water floats.

idk.hint: Is it about size, weight or density?

steps.answerWhy: Floating depends on density: an object less dense than water floats, whatever its size.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: which is true of the atmosphere?

options.text: It is thin compared with the size of the Earth
It reaches as far as the Moon
It is thicker than the Earth is wide

steps.right: Yes: the atmosphere is a thin layer of air round the Earth.

wrong.other: Not quite: it is thin compared with the size of the Earth.
wrong.moon: Not quite: the Moon is far beyond the air. The atmosphere is a thin layer round the Earth.
wrong.thick: Not quite: the atmosphere is a thin layer, much thinner than the Earth is wide.

idk.hint: Think of a layer of air like the skin on an apple.

steps.answerWhy: The atmosphere is a thin layer of air, thin compared with the size of the Earth.
